clinicalPearls: Disseminated gonococcal infection results from bloodstream spread of Neisseria gonorrhoeae, often from an asymptomatic mucosal focus in the genital tract, rectum, or pharynx
It classically presents in one of two overlapping forms: an arthritis-dermatitis (bacteraemic) syndrome and a localised purulent (septic) arthritis

The arthritis-dermatitis form features migratory or additive polyarthralgia, tenosynovitis (often of the wrists, hands, and ankles), and scattered painful pustular or haemorrhagic skin lesions, usually with negative synovial cultures
The purulent-arthritis form produces a frankly septic mono- or oligoarthritis with an inflammatory effusion from which the organism is more often recovered
Because the responsible mucosal infection is frequently silent, a high index of suspicion and a full sexual history are needed, and it is comparatively more common in women

Blood, synovial fluid, skin lesions, and all relevant mucosal sites should be sampled, using culture and nucleic acid amplification testing, with antimicrobial susceptibility testing given rising resistance
Treatment is with a parenteral third-generation cephalosporin such as ceftriaxone, with joint drainage for purulent arthritis and coverage for co-existing chlamydia as guided by local policy

Deficiency of terminal complement components (and functional or anatomical asplenia) predisposes to recurrent or disseminated neisserial infection and should prompt complement screening in recurrent cases
reference.pathophysiology: Disseminated gonococcal infection occurs when Neisseria gonorrhoeae invades from a mucosal surface into the bloodstream, a step favoured by particular gonococcal strains that resist normal serum bactericidal activity and by host factors. Circulating organisms and the immune response to them seed the skin, tenosynovium, and joints, producing an immune-complex-influenced arthritis-dermatitis picture in the early bacteraemic phase and, later or in other patients, direct bacterial seeding of a joint with suppurative arthritis. The organism's marked antigenic variation helps it evade immunity, while an intact terminal complement (membrane attack complex) pathway is critical for killing Neisseria, so individuals deficient in these complement components are strikingly susceptible to disseminated and recurrent neisserial disease.
additionalDifferentials: Non-gonococcal septic arthritis (for example Staphylococcus aureus)
Reactive arthritis following genitourinary or enteric infection
Crystal arthropathy such as gout or pseudogout
Acute rheumatological disease such as systemic lupus erythematosus or rheumatoid flare
Meningococcaemia or other bacteraemia with skin lesions
Viral arthritis (for example parvovirus or hepatitis B)
additionalInvestigations: Blood cultures during the bacteraemic phase
Synovial fluid aspiration for cell count, Gram stain, culture, and nucleic acid amplification testing
Nucleic acid amplification testing and culture from genital, rectal, and pharyngeal mucosal sites
Gram stain and culture of skin lesion aspirate or swab
Antimicrobial susceptibility testing of gonococcal isolates given rising resistance
Screening for coexisting sexually transmitted infections including chlamydia, HIV, and syphilis
Terminal complement (for example CH50) screening in recurrent disseminated neisserial infection
redFlags: Features suggesting gonococcal endocarditis or meningitis
A hot, swollen, immobile joint indicating septic arthritis requiring urgent drainage
Recurrent disseminated neisserial infection pointing to terminal complement deficiency
Rapidly evolving haemorrhagic or necrotic skin lesions
reference.prognosis: With prompt parenteral antibiotics and, where needed, joint drainage the outlook is generally very good and most patients recover fully, though delayed treatment of purulent arthritis can cause lasting joint damage, and rare complications such as endocarditis or meningitis carry higher risk.
pitfalls: Not considering disseminated gonococcal infection in a sexually active patient with polyarthralgia, tenosynovitis, and pustular skin lesions
Excluding the diagnosis because genital symptoms or mucosal cultures are absent, when the source is often silent
Omitting sampling of all relevant mucosal sites and skin lesions, reducing diagnostic yield
Failing to screen for terminal complement deficiency in recurrent cases
Overlooking concurrent chlamydia or other sexually transmitted infection
references: BASHH UK national guideline for the management of gonorrhoea in adults
CDC Sexually Transmitted Infections Treatment Guidelines
Mandell, Douglas, and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
management: Prompt parenteral third-generation cephalosporin (ceftriaxone) is the mainstay, guided by susceptibility testing given rising resistance
Add empirical treatment for chlamydia co-infection
Drain a purulent septic joint by aspiration or arthroscopic washout
Step down to oral therapy once clinically improving to complete an adequate course
Screen and treat for concurrent sexually transmitted infections including HIV, syphilis, and chlamydia, and treat sexual partners
Investigate for terminal complement deficiency in recurrent disseminated Neisseria infection
Provide supportive analgesia with joint rest and physiotherapy for arthritis
